lessons.title: Defining a function and returning a value
lessons.body:
A function is defined with `def`. Its indented body runs each time the function is called. A `return` statement ends the call and sends a value back to the caller. A function that reaches its end without `return` gives back `None`.

```python
def double(x):
    return x * 2

result = double(4) + 1
```

`double(4)` produces 8 for the caller to use. `print` only displays a value; it does not send the value back.

lessons.title: Parameters, arguments, and local names
lessons.body:
A parameter is a name that receives an argument when the function is called. Assigning to a name inside a function body makes that name local to the call, so a global name with the same spelling is not changed. Keyword arguments name the parameter they fill, and a parameter may have a default value.

```python
total = 10

def add_five(total):
    total = total + 5
    return total

add_five(1)   # returns 6; the global total is still 10
```

lessons.title: A function that calls itself
The base case stops the recursion
lessons.body:
The base case is the branch that returns without making another recursive call. Without a base case, every call makes another call and the chain never ends. Python limits how deep the call stack may grow. When that depth is exceeded, Python raises `RecursionError`. `sys.getrecursionlimit()` reports the current limit.

```python
def f(n):
    if n == 0: return 1
    return n * f(n - 1)
```

In `f`, the test `n == 0` is the base case.

items.prompt: Which statement sends a value back to the caller of a function?

hints.text: Look for the keyword that ends a function call with a value.
print shows a value on screen; it does not send the value back.
return total sends total back to the caller.

items.prompt: After this code runs, what is the value of result?

hints.text: Evaluate double(7) first.
double(7) returns 7 * 2.
double(7) is 14, so result is 14 + 1, which is 15.

items.prompt: After this code runs, what is the value of result?

hints.text: Work out area(3, 4) first.
area(3, 4) returns 3 * 4, which is 12.
12 - 2 is 10, so result is 10.

items.prompt: After this code runs, what is the value of result?
items.body:
total = 10
def add_five(total):
    total = total + 5
    return total
result = add_five(1)

hints.text: The parameter total is a new local name inside the function.
add_five(1) computes 1 + 5 inside its own call.
add_five(1) returns 6, so result is 6.

items.prompt: After this code runs, what is the value of the global name total?
items.body:
total = 10
def add_five(total):
    total = total + 5
    return total
add_five(1)

hints.text: Assignments inside add_five do not rebind the global name.
The total inside the function is local; the global total was set to 10 before the call.
The global total is still 10, so the answer is 10.

items.prompt: In your own words, what makes a function recursive, and what must stop its calls?

rubric.annotated_example: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. A stopping condition returns without another self-call, so the chain can unwind.
common_mistakes: Saying only that the function repeats does not identify a self-call.
Leaving out the stopping condition does not explain why calls finish.

criteria.description: Says the function calls itself on a smaller or simpler version of the problem.
Says some condition must stop the calls, or they never end.

hints.text: Think about what each call does with a smaller input.
Say what makes the function call itself and what stops it.
A recursive function calls itself on a simpler version of the problem, and a stopping condition must end the calls.

items.prompt: In a recursive function, which part stops the repeated calls?

hints.text: Think about what happens when the calls must stop.
The recursive call keeps going; something else must stop it.
The base case is the condition that returns without another call.

items.prompt: Explain what goes wrong if a recursive function has no base case.

rubric.annotated_example: Without a base case, each call makes another call without a stopping return. Python eventually raises RecursionError when the recursion depth limit is reached.
common_mistakes: A missing base case does not simply return None.
RecursionError is an observed runtime limit, not a successful stopping rule.

criteria.description: States that without a base case the calls never reach a stopping point.
Mentions that Python raises RecursionError once the recursion depth limit is exceeded.

hints.text: Ask what happens to each new call when no call ever returns without recursing.
Mention the stopping point and what Python does when the depth limit is exceeded.
Without a base case the calls never reach a stopping point, so the call stack grows until Python raises RecursionError.

items.prompt: Write a recursive function sum_list(items) that returns the sum of a list of numbers. Do not use a loop.

common_mistakes: Recursing on the same list does not move toward the empty base case.
A branch with no return value cannot supply the sum to its caller.

criteria.description: Handles the empty list with a base case that returns a value without recursing.
The recursive case combines the first item with a recursive call on the rest of the list.
Each recursive call receives a shorter list, so the calls reach the base case.

hints.text: Start with the base case for an empty list.
The recursive case can add the first item to the sum of the rest.
Handle [] by returning 0; otherwise return items[0] + sum_list(items[1:]).
